Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 42, verses 1–5:

(p-498) In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

Tafsir of Surah al-Shura

This surah is Meccan by the consensus of most exegetes. Muqatil said: "It contains a Medinan part," namely [His saying, exalted is He] ﴿That is what Allah gives good news of to His servants who believe and do righteous deeds﴾ [al-Shura: 23] up to His saying ﴿the secrets of the breasts﴾ [al-Shura: 24], and His saying, exalted is He, ﴿And those who, when tyranny afflicts them﴾ [al-Shura: 39] up to His saying, exalted is He, ﴿any way [against them]﴾ [al-Shura: 41]. Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, said in the book of al-Tha'labi: that ﴿Ha Mim﴾ [Ghafir: 1] ﴿The revelation of the Book is from Allah, the Mighty, the All-Knowing﴾ [Ghafir: 2] — these letters themselves were revealed in all the books of Allah sent down to every prophet to whom a Book was revealed. Therefore Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿Thus does He reveal to you, and to those before you, Allah﴾.

The words of the Most High:

﴿Ha Mim﴾ ﴿'Ayn Sin Qaf﴾ ﴿Thus does He reveal to you, and to those before you, Allah, the Mighty, the Wise﴾ ﴿To Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth, and He is the Most High, the Most Great﴾ ﴿The heavens are almost rent asunder from above them, while the angels glorify the praise of their Lord and seek forgiveness for those on the earth. Unquestionably, Allah is the Forgiving, the Merciful﴾

It is said: [Ha] is separated from ['Ayn Sin Qaf] and it was not done so with [Kaf Ha Ya 'Ayn Sad], so that these would take the same course as their sisters, the Ha Mim surahs. The majority of readers recite "Ha 'Ayn Sin Qaf," while Ibn Mas'ud and Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them, recited [Ha Sin Qaf] with the dropping of "'Ayn." The views concerning these are like the views concerning the openings of the surahs. Huzayfah narrated a hadith on this, the gist of which is: «There will be in this community two cities, a river running between them in the east; one of them will perish at night, and then the other will wake up safe. The tyrants of both cities will gather there, astonished at its safety, and then it will perish on the following night.» It is also said that "Ha" means: "this matter has been decreed" (ḥumma), "'Ayn" means: (p-499) "justice from Allah," "Sin" means: "that will happen," and "Qaf" means: "that will befall them." It is also narrated that 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with him, used to derive knowledge of trials and wars from these letters that occur at the openings of the surahs.

The kaf in His saying ﴿"Thus"﴾ is an adjective of an omitted verbal noun (masdar), and the reference of "Thus" (dhalika) varies according to the views on the letters. The majority of readers recite "yuhi" with the ya', attributing the verb to Allah, the Most High, and this is the reading of al-Hasan, al-A'raj, Abu Ja'far, al-Jahdari, 'Isa, Talhah, and al-A'mash. Abu Haywah and al-A'sha, from Abu Bakr, from 'Asim, recited "nuhi" with the nun of majesty, and then His saying, exalted is He, ﴿"Allah"﴾ would be a beginning (mubtada') whose predicate is ﴿"the Mighty"﴾, and it is possible that its predicate is ﴿To Him belongs whatever is in the heavens﴾. Ibn Kathir alone recited "yuha" with the ya' and a fatha on the ha', with the verb in the passive form, and this is the reading of Mujahid; the implied meaning is: "the Qur'an is revealed to you, revealed by Allah, the Most High," as the poet said:

"Let Yazid the suppliant weep for a dispute."

And from this is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿He is glorified therein in the mornings and evenings by men﴾ [al-Nur: 36–37]. And His saying, exalted is He, ﴿and to those before you﴾ means: the prophets to whom the Books were sent down.

His saying, exalted is He, ﴿To Him belongs whatever is in the heavens﴾ means: the dominion, the creation, and the origination. "Al-'Aliyy" (the Most High) is from the loftiness of rank and authority, and "al-'Azim" (the Most Great) likewise; it is not a loftiness of distance nor a greatness of physical mass, exalted is Allah above that. Nafi' and al-Kisa'i recited "yakadu" with the ya'. Ibn Kathir, Ibn 'Amir, Hamzah, Abu 'Amr, and 'Asim recited "takadu" with the ta'. Ibn Kathir, Ibn 'Amir, Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, Nafi', Ibn 'Abbas, Abu Ja'far, Shaybah, and Qatadah recited "yatafattarna" from "tafattur," which is the intransitive form of "fattara," and Abu 'Amr, 'Asim, al-Hasan, al-A'raj, Abu Raja', and al-Jahdari recited [yanfatirna] from "infitar," which is also the intransitive form of "fattara." The meaning in both is: they split and crack from the swiftness of their motion, out of submission and fear of the authority of Allah, the Most High, and out of glorification and obedience to Him. What has been reported from the exegetes here about weight and the like is rejected, because Allah, the Most High, is not described by it. His saying, exalted is He, ﴿from above them﴾ means: from above them. Al-Akhfash 'Ali ibn Sulayman said: the pronoun refers to the disbelievers.

Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

The meaning is: from above the sects and the groups of deviators, because of whose statements the heavens are almost rent asunder. On this view, this verse is like the verse in [Kaf Ha Ya 'Ayn Sad] [Maryam: 1]. Another group said: the meaning is: from above the earths, since the earth has already been mentioned. al-Zajjaj mentioned that it was read: "yatafattarna mimman fawqahunna."

His saying, exalted is He, ﴿while the angels glorify the praise of their Lord﴾, it is said: its meaning is that they say "Subhan Allah"; it is also said its meaning is that they pray to their Lord. His saying, exalted is He, ﴿and seek forgiveness for those on the earth﴾: one group said: this is abrogated by His saying, exalted is He, in another verse: ﴿and seek forgiveness for those who believe﴾ [Ghafir: 7].

(p-501) Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This is a weak view, because abrogation is not conceivable in reports.

Al-Suddi said, in substance: the apparent meaning of the verse is general, but its meaning is specific to the believers, as if He had said: "and they seek forgiveness for those on the earth among the believers," since the disbelievers are under the curse of Allah, the angels, and all people. Another group said: rather, it remains general, but the angels' seeking forgiveness is not a request for Allah's forgiveness for the disbelievers so that they remain disbelievers; rather their seeking forgiveness for them means a request for guidance that leads to their forgiveness. It is as if the angels say: "O Allah, guide the people of the earth and forgive them." This interpretation is supported by the emphasis on the attributes of forgiveness and mercy for Himself by the opening of the statement, which is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Unquestionably, Allah is the Forgiving, the Merciful﴾. That is, since seeking forgiveness for everyone on the earth is unlikely to be granted, the Mighty and Majestic prepared the listener's soul by opening the speech, saying: "Unquestionably, Allah is the One who is asked this of Him, since these are His attributes, and He, glory be to Him, is the Possessor of forgiveness."

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 42, verses 6–9:

His the Exalted and Majestic's saying:

﴿And those who take protectors other than Him—Allah is Watchful over them, and you are not a guardian over them.﴾ ﴿And thus We have revealed to you an Arabic Qur'an, that you may warn the Mother of Cities (Makkah) and those around it, and warn of the Day of Assembly, about which there is no doubt: a party will be in the Garden and a party in the Blaze.﴾ ﴿And had Allah willed, He would have made them one community, but He admits whom He wills into His mercy; and the wrongdoers—they have no protector nor helper.﴾ ﴿Or have they taken protectors other than Him? But Allah—He is the Protector, and He gives life to the dead, and He is Able over all things.﴾

This verse is a consolation to the Prophet ﷺ, a warning to the disbelievers, and a removal from the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) of all burdens other than conveying the message alone, so that he would not be preoccupied with the non-belief of the Quraysh and others. So the Exalted said to His Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him): Indeed, those who have taken idols and images as protectors besides Allah—Allah is the Watchful over them: He counts their deeds, He recompenses them for them with the punishment of the Hereafter. As for you, you are not a "wakil" (guardian) over them, nor one who is bound to their affair until they believe. And "al-wakil" means one who stands firmly over a matter. Whatever in this wording suggests leniency is abrogated by the verse of the sword.

Then the Exalted said: ﴿And thus We have revealed to you﴾, i.e., just as We have decreed your affair in this manner and carried it out in this form, thus We have revealed to you an Arabic Qur'an, clarifying for them, which they do not need anything else alongside; for its understanding is accessible to them, and He did not charge you with anything except warning those mentioned. "Umm al-Qura" is Makkah, and what is intended is its people, which is why "man" is conjoined to it; and it is, for the most part, used for those who have reason. "Yawm al-jam'" is the Day of Resurrection. In "tundhira" he limited himself to the first object, because the meaning is: the Mother of Cities is warned of the punishment, and you warn the people on the Day of Assembly, due to the gathering of the people of the earth with the people of the heavens, or due to the gathering of the children of Adam for the Reckoning. The Exalted's saying ﴿there is no doubt about it﴾ means in its very essence and reality, and the disbelievers' doubt about it does not restrict it.

The Exalted's saying "a party" is in the nominative as the predicate of an implied subject, as if the Exalted said: they are a party in the Garden and a party in the Blaze.

Then the Blessed and Exalted strengthened the consolation of His Prophet ﷺ by informing him that the matter is contingent upon the will of Allah, regarding their belief or their disbelief, and that if He had willed them to be one community, He would have gathered them upon it; but He admits into His mercy whoever happiness has preceded for him with Him, and facilitates for him in this world the deeds of the people of happiness; and that the wrongdoers in disbelief, who are facilitated for the deeds of wretchedness, have no protector nor helper.

The Exalted's saying ﴿"Or have they taken"﴾ is a statement disconnected from what precedes it, and it is not an equation (mu'adala); rather, the speech is as if it turned away from an argument of theirs or a established assertion, and said: "Bal (rather), they have taken." This is the well-known view of the grammarians regarding such a case. Some of them held that this "am" is in the position of the interrogative alif without implying a turning away. Then the Exalted affirmed the ruling that He, Mighty and Majestic, is the Protector whose protection benefits, and that He is the One who gives life to the dead, gathers them to the Hereafter and resurrects them from their graves, and that His power over all things gives this and necessitates it.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 42, verses 10–12:

Allah's, the Exalted and Majestic, saying:

﴿Whatever you dispute about, its judgment rests with Allah. That is Allah, my Lord; upon Him I rely, and to Him I turn in repentance.﴾ ﴿Originator of the heavens and the earth. He made for you mates from among yourselves, and of the cattle, mates; He multiplies you thereby. Nothing is like Him, and He is the All-Hearing, the All-Seeing.﴾ ﴿To Him belong the keys of the heavens and the earth. He extends provision to whomever He wills and restricts it. Indeed, He is All-Knowing of everything.﴾

The meaning: Say, O Muhammad: "Whatever you dispute about, O people, of denial and affirmation, faith and disbelief, and other than that, the judgment regarding it and the recompense for it are not up to me and not in my hand. Rather, that is up to Allah, whose attributes are what He mentioned of giving life to the dead and power over everything." Then He said: "That is Allah, my Lord; upon Him is my reliance, to Him is my turning back and my return." He is the Originator of the heavens and the earth, meaning the one who brings them into being and creates them, splitting some of them from others.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿He made for you mates from among yourselves﴾ means: He made the human being's female a mate, and by this blessing the multiplication (dhar') came about. Here "azwaj" (mates) does not mean "types" (anwa'). As for the "azwaj" mentioned together with the cattle, the apparent and more consistent reading is also that it means females and males (the pairs), though it may be understood as "types." The first is more apparent.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿He multiplies you thereby﴾ means: He creates you as offspring after offspring and generation after generation, as Mujahid and the people said. The word "dhara'a" adds to the word "khalaqa" (created) another meaning not present in "khalaqa," namely the succession of strata over the passage of time. The pronoun in "fihi" (thereby) refers to the "making" (ja'l) implied in His saying ﴿He made for you﴾. This is like saying: "I spoke to Zayd a speech, I honoured him in it." Al-Utbi said: the pronoun refers to marriage (tazwij). The word "fi" (in) is shared among several meanings, though its original sense is container, and examination in every case returns to that sense.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Nothing is like Him﴾: the kaf (like) is a particle of emphasis (ta'kid) for the comparison, so the negation of comparison is at its most emphatic. This is because you say: "Zayd is like ('ka') 'Amr," and "Zayd is the like of ('mithl') 'Amr." But when you want the complete hyperbole, you say: "Zayd is like the like of ('ka-mithl') 'Amr." From this is the saying of Aws ibn Hajar:

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 42, verses 13–14:

His Exalted and Majestic saying:

﴿He has ordained for you of the religion what He enjoined upon Noah, and that which We have revealed to you, and what We enjoined upon Abraham, Moses and Jesus: that you should establish the religion and not be divided therein. Hard for the polytheists is that to which you call them. Allah chooses for Himself whom He wills and guides to Himself whoever turns back (in repentance).﴾ ﴿And they did not become divided except after knowledge had come to them, out of mutual insolence. And had it not been for a word that preceded from your Lord for an appointed term, it would have been judged between them. And indeed, those who were given the Scripture after them are in disquieting doubt concerning it.﴾

The meaning: Allah the Exalted has ordained for you, and made clear, from among the beliefs and tawhid, what He enjoined upon Noah before. His saying ﴿"and that which"﴾ is a conjunction upon "mā" (what). Likewise, what is mentioned after "min" (of), the establishment of the religion, is a legislation upon which the prophets agreed. This concerns the beliefs, or the sum of their matter, because every prophethood contains beliefs and rulings. The meaning therefore becomes: He ordained for you a legislation (shir'a) which is like the legislation of Noah, Abraham, Moses and Jesus, peace be upon them, in that it has the well-known beliefs that are in every prophecy, and rulings, as all of those were. On this basis is explained what al-Tabari related from Qatada, who said: ﴿what He enjoined upon Noah﴾ means: the lawful and the unlawful. Upon this it is narrated that Noah, peace be upon him, was the first to bring the prohibition of daughters and mothers. As for the rulings taken individually, they differ in the legislations, and these are what is meant in His saying: ﴿For each of you We have appointed a law (shir'a) and a path (minhaj)﴾ [al-Ma'ida: 48]. The "an" in His saying ﴿that you should establish the religion﴾ may be in a position of accusative as a substitute (badal) for "mā"; it may be in a position of genitive as a substitute for the pronoun in "bihi" (with it); or in a position of nominative as the predicate of an implied subject, its implied form being: "that is" (dhalika) an, and it may be an explanatory "an" with the meaning of "i.e." (ay) having no place in i'rab (grammatical case). "Establishing the religion" is the tawhid of Allah the Exalted and the rejection of whatever is other than Him.

His saying ﴿and do not be divided﴾ is a prohibition of the destructive kind of division into schools and sects, and all good lies in unity and the unification of the word. Then Allah the Exalted informed His Prophet, peace be upon him, of the difficulty of the position of this call to establish the religion among the polytheists who worship idols. Qatada said: "There is no god but Allah" was hard upon them, and Allah refused except to make it victorious and manifest. Then Allah the Exalted consoled him concerning them with His saying: ﴿Allah chooses﴾, i.e., selects and chooses. Mujahid and others said this. And "yunib" means: he returns from disbelief, eagerly seeks goodness and pursues it.

His saying ﴿and do not be divided﴾ is an expression whose address includes the disbelieving Arabs, the Jews and the Christians, and every one invited to Islam. Therefore it was fitting to say ﴿what divided﴾, meaning by that: the early Jews and Christians. The knowledge that came to them is what had been established in their souls of the knowledge of the Books of Allah the Exalted, so some of them transgressed against others, and that led them to disagreement in opinion. As for "the word that preceded" (al-kalima al-sabiqa), the commentators said: it is Allah's decree, the Exalted, that their recompense occurs only in the Hereafter; had it not been for that, He would have judged between them in this world and the true would have overcome the falsifier.

His saying ﴿And indeed, those who were given the Scripture﴾ is a reference to the contemporaries of Muhammad (ﷺ) among the Jews and Christians. It has been said that it refers to the Arabs. "Al-Kitab" is the Qur'an. The pronoun in His saying ﴿in doubt﴾ may refer back to "al-Kitab", or to Muhammad (ﷺ), or to "the appointed term"; that is, in doubt about the Resurrection according to the view of those who take the reference to be to the Arabs. Describing the doubt as ﴿disquieting﴾ is an intensification concerning it.

Unquestionably, those who dispute concerning the Hour are in far-off error.﴾ ﴿Allah is Subtle toward His servants; He provides for whom He wills, and He is the Strong, the Mighty.﴾ ﴿Whoever desires the tilth of the Hereafter, We increase for him in his tilth; and whoever desires the tilth of this world, We give him of it, but he has no share in the Hereafter.﴾

The word "أم" here is disjunctive (*munqati'a*), not coordinating (*mu'adila*), and it is to be understood as "بل" (rather) together with the interrogative alif (*alif al-istifham*).

Regarding "al-shuraka'" (the partners) in this verse, it is possible that the intended meaning is the devils and the misguiding ones among their forefathers. The pronoun in "لهم" would then refer to the disbelievers contemporary with Muhammad (ﷺ), meaning: the partners prescribed for them what Allah had not permitted. The partnership here is then one of disbelief and misguidance, not the partnership of associating others with Allah (*shirk*). It is also possible that the intended meaning of "al-shuraka'" is the idols and idols/images, in the sense: "Or do they have idols which they have made partners to Allah in His divinity?" The pronoun in "shara'u" (they prescribed) would then refer to these contemporary disbelievers and their forefathers, and the pronoun in "lahum" to the idols that are the partners. That is, these disbelievers prescribed for their idols and images what Allah the Exalted had not permitted. "Shara'u" means: they established, followed, and laid down. "Al-din" (religion) here means customs, rulings, and conduct, and this also includes beliefs, because in all of these they laid down practices. As for beliefs, there is their saying that the idols are gods, their saying that they worship the idols so that they may draw near to Allah, and other such things. As for rulings, there are such things as the *bahira*, the *wasila*, and the *ham*, and other such things of the *sawa'ib* (free-roaming animals) and the like. The word "al-idhn" (permission) in this verse means command.

"Kalimat al-fasl" (the decisive word) refers to what preceded from the decree of Allah the Exalted that He would delay their punishment until the Hereafter. "Al-qada' baynahum" (the judgment between them) refers to their punishment in this world and their requital. Most of the reciters read "wa inna al-zalimin" with a kasra on the hamza, as a new and independent sentence. Muslim ibn Jundab read it with a fatha on the hamza. In that reading it is in the place of the nominative, coordinated with "kalimat," and the meaning is: "and that the wrongdoers will have in the Hereafter a painful punishment."

As for the words of the Exalted, ﴿You see the wrongdoers fearful﴾, this is sight of the eye (*ru'yat basar*). "Al-zalimin" is the object, and "mushfiqin" is a circumstantial state (*hal*). There is no praise for them in this fear, because they feared only when it descended upon them and befell them. They are unlike the believers who, in this world, fear the Hour, as has already been mentioned. The words of the Exalted, ﴿while it befalls them﴾, are in the place of a circumstantial state. "Al-rawdat" (meadows) are the pleasant, verdant, and beautiful places, which are generally elevated in usage. They are praised among the Arabs and others. Among this is the words of the Exalted, ﴿like a garden on a height﴾ [al-Baqarah: 265]. Among this is their preference for the meadows of al-Huzn because of the excellence of their air. Al-Tabari said: The Arabs do not call a place of trees "riyad."

The words of the Exalted, ﴿That is what Allah gives good news of to His servants﴾, refer to His saying in another verse: ﴿And give good news to the believers that they will have from Allah a great bounty﴾ [al-Ahzab: 47]. Most of the reciters read "yubashshiru" with a damma on the yaa', a fatha on the baa', and a shadda on the shin with a kasra, as a transitive form with intensification (*ta'diya wa tad'if*). Mujahid and Humayd read "yubshiru" with a damma on the yaa', a sukun on the baa', and a kasra on the shin, as transitive through the hamza. Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn Ya'mur, Ibn Abi Ishaq, al-Jahdari, al-A'mash, and Talha read "yabshuru" with a fatha on the yaa' and a damma on the shin, and this is reported from Ibn Kathir. Al-Jahdari, in explaining it, said: you see the radiance in the faces.

As for the words of the Exalted, ﴿Say: I do not ask you for it any reward except affection among relatives﴾, people differed about its meaning. Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, and others said: it is a Meccan verse, revealed at the beginning of Islam, and its meaning is seeking protection from the evil of the disbelievers and repelling their harm. That is: I do not ask you, for the Qur'an, the religion, and the calling to Allah the Exalted, anything except that you show affection to me because of the kinship between me and you, so that you refrain from harming me. Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn Ishaq, and Qatada said: there was no clan in Quraysh except that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) had a lineage or marriage tie with it. So the verse, on this interpretation, is an appeal for compassion, a request for repelling harm, and a seeking of safety from them. All of this is abrogated by the verse of the sword (*ayat al-sayf*). This interpretation may also be taken to mean a request for their support: that is, I do not ask you for a payment or anything, except that you show affection to me because of my kinship with you, and that you be closer to me than others.

Mujahid said: except that you join my kinship by following me. Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, also said something that implies it is a Medinan verse, and its occasion was that some young men of the Ansar boasted over the Muhajirun and inclined their speech against Quraysh; so the verse was revealed concerning that, in the sense: except that you show affection to me, so that you observe my kinship and protect me among them. 'Ali ibn al-Husayn ibn 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with them, said this meaning concerning the verse, and he cited the verse when he was led as a captive to Syria. This is also the interpretation of Ibn Jubayr and 'Amr ibn Shu'ayb. According to this interpretation, Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, said: "It was said: O Messenger of Allah, who are your relatives whose affection we were commanded to show? He said: 'Ali, Fatima, and their two sons." It was also said: it refers to the descendants of 'Abd al-Muttalib.

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

All of Quraysh is, in my view, kin, although they differ in their merit. It has been related from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "Whoever dies loving the family of Muhammad dies as a martyr, and whoever dies hating them will not smell the fragrance of Paradise." Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, also said in the book of al-Tha'labi: the cause of this verse was that "the Ansar gathered wealth for the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and brought it to him, but he returned it to them, and the verse was revealed concerning that." Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, also said: the meaning of the verse is: "Of the kinship of obedience and drawing near to Allah the Exalted," as if he said: "except that you show affection to me, because I am the nearest of you to Allah the Exalted, and I wish to guide you and call you to it." Al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan said: its meaning is: except that you seek affection toward Allah the Exalted by drawing near to Him. 'Abd Allah ibn al-Qasim said, in the book of al-Tabari: the meaning of the verse is: except that you show affection to one another and join your relationships; so the verse, on this interpretation, is a command to maintain the ties of kinship.

Al-Naqqash related from Ibn 'Abbas, Muqatil, al-Kalbi, and al-Suddi that the verse is abrogated by the words of the Exalted in Surah Saba': ﴿Say: whatever reward I have asked of you, it is for you﴾ [Saba': 47]. The correct view, however, is that it is muhkam (not abrogated). On either view, the exception is disjunctive, and "illa" has the meaning of "lakin" (but).

"Yaqtarif" means: he earns. A man is called *qirfa* if he is a crafty earner. One group read "nazid" as "yazid," attributing the verb to Allah the Exalted. Most of the reciters read "nazid" with the plural "we" of majesty. The increase in goodness is the multiplication that Allah the Exalted promised to the believing among His servants, as al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan said. "Ghafur" means: one who covers the faults of His servants. "Shakur" means: one who rewards even the smallest good, so that no deed of the doer is lost before Him.

Then God mentioned the blessing in His bestowal of accepting repentance from His servants. The acceptance of repentance regarding what the servant undertakes in his time and actions is affirmed by this verse. **Ibn ʿAṭiyya:** The words of the Exalted:

﴿It is He who sends down the rain after they have despaired, and spreads His mercy. And He is the Protector, the Praiseworthy.﴾ ﴿And among His signs is the creation of the heavens and the earth, and of the living creatures He has dispersed in them. And He is able to gather them whenever He wills.﴾ ﴿Whatever affliction befalls you is because of what your hands have earned, and He pardons much.﴾ ﴿You cannot escape in the earth, and you have no protector or helper besides Allah.﴾ ﴿And among His signs are the ships on the sea, like mountains.﴾ ﴿If He wills, He stills the wind, and they remain motionless on its surface. Indeed, in that are signs for everyone who is patient and grateful.﴾

This is an enumeration of the blessings of Allah the Exalted, which point to His oneness, and that He is the God who alone deserves to be worshipped, to the exclusion of rival gods. The reading "yunazzilu" (with the doubled zay) is that of the majority of the readers (of the Qur'an). Ibn Wathhab, al-Aʿmash, and (a reading) transmitted from Abu ʿAmr read "yunzilu" (with a single zay). Abu Ḥatim preferred this reading. The majority of people read "qanaṭū" with a fatḥa on the nūn, while Yaḥyā ibn Wathhāb and al-Aʿmash read it with a kasra on the nūn. This has been mentioned before, and both forms are dialectal variants: qanaṭa and qanira (to despair).

It is related that ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb, may Allah be pleased with him, was told: "The land has become barren and the people have despaired." He said: "Then they will be given rain," meaning that relief comes at the time of hardship.

The commentators differed concerning the words of the Exalted: ﴿and spreads His mercy﴾. One group said: by "mercy" He means rain, and He has enumerated one blessing with two expressions, the second of which emphasises the first. Another group said: the mercy in this place is the sun. This is then an enumeration of a different blessing from the first. The reason is that when rain falls after despair, it is well received, but when it continues it becomes wearisome, so the sun comes after it, which is of great benefit. The words of the Exalted: ﴿He is the Protector, the Praiseworthy﴾ mean that from these acts of His, He is the one who benefits when He is an ally, and His acts and blessings are praised, unlike those idols of yours that neither harm nor benefit.

Then the Exalted mentioned the greatest sign and the handiwork that points to the Maker, which is His creation of the heavens and the earth. As for the words of the Exalted: ﴿and of the living creatures He has dispersed in them﴾, this can be interpreted in several ways. One is that He means one of the two (heavens or earth) but mentions both, as the Exalted said: ﴿From both of them come forth pearls and coral﴾ (Qur'an 55:22), while in fact they come forth only from the salt water. Another is that Allah the Exalted created the heavens and dispersed creatures in them that we do not know. Another is that He means the animals found in the clouds, which sometimes occur, such as frogs and the like, since the cloud is included in the name "sky." Al-Ṭabarī related from Mujāhid that he said, in explaining the words ﴿and of the living creatures He has dispersed in them﴾, that they are humans and angels.

The Qāḍī Abū Muḥammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

It is far-fetched, and not in accordance with the usage of the language, for the word "dābba" (living creature) to apply to angels.

The words of the Exalted: ﴿And He is able to gather them﴾ mean: on the Day of Resurrection, at the gathering from the graves.

The words of the Exalted: ﴿Whatever affliction befalls you﴾: the majority of readers read "fa-bimā" with a fāʾ (so the reading is "fa-bimā kasabat"), and it is so in most of the codices. Nāfiʿ, Ibn ʿĀmir, Abū Jaʿfar, and Shayba read "bimā" without a fāʾ. Al-Zajjāj related that Abū Jaʿfar and others among the people of Medina affirmed the fāʾ. Abū ʿAlī al-Fārisī said: The verb "aṣāba" in the phrase "mā aṣāba" may be in the jussive position, with "mā" being conditional. In this case, according to Sībawayh, it is not permitted to omit the fāʾ. Abū al-Ḥasan al-Akhfash and some of the Baghdadis permitted its omission, on the basis that it is implied in meaning. It is also possible that the verb "aṣāba" is a relative clause (ṣila) for "mā," and "mā" then means "alladhī" (that which). In this case, it is permitted to omit the fāʾ or to keep it. However, the meaning of the sentence with the fāʾ present involves necessary implication: that is, were it not for your earning, no affliction would have befallen you, and affliction only occurs because of what the hands have earned. The meaning of the sentence with the fāʾ omitted may include that implication, or it may be free of it.

In this verse, however, the implication is consistent whether the fāʾ is present or omitted. As for the meaning of the verse, people have differed about it. One group said: it is an announcement from Allah the Exalted that the calamities and afflictions in this world are only a recompense from Allah the Exalted for a person's sins and a purification of his wrongdoings, and that Allah the Exalted pardons much, so that he is not punished for it with affliction. It was said to Abū Sulaymān al-Dārānī: "What is the matter with the excellent people that they do not blame those who wrong them?" He said: "Because they know that Allah the Exalted is the One who tested them with their sins." It is related from ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib, may Allah be pleased with him, from the Prophet (ﷺ), that he said: "Allah is too generous to punish His servant in this world for what his hands have earned." Al-Ḥasan ibn Abī al-Ḥasan said: The meaning of the verse concerns the prescribed punishments (ḥudūd). That is: whatever affliction (ḥadd) of the prescribed punishments of Allah, blessed and exalted is He, befalls you (and that is an affliction that descends upon the person himself), then it is because of what your hands have earned, and Allah, glorified is He, pardons much, so He conceals it for the servant so that the prescribed punishment is not imposed on him. Then the Exalted informed about the limitation and weakness of the son of Adam, and that he is within the grasp of power, that the pursuit of his Lord, mighty and majestic is He, cannot be frustrated, and that escape from Him is not possible for him.

"Al-Jawārī" is the plural of "jāriya," which means a ship. Nāfiʿ, ʿĀṣim, Abū Jaʿfar, and Shayba read "al-jawārī" with the yāʾ. Some retained it both in connection and at a pause on the rāʾ. ʿĀṣim also read it with the yāʾ omitted both in connection and at a pause. Abū Ḥātim said: "We retain it in every case." "Al-aʿlām" means mountains, and from it comes the saying of al-Khansāʾ:

*Indeed Ṣakhr, by him the rightly guided take their lead,*
*as if he were a beacon with fire at its top.*

And from it comes the proverb: "When they passed a mountain, another mountain appeared." So the sailing of ships on the water is a great sign, and the subjection of the wind for that is a blessing from Him, the Exalted. And if He willed to still the wind from them, they would remain motionless, that is, they would stand still and not move, and no purpose would be accomplished by them. Abū ʿAmr and ʿĀṣim read "al-rīḥ" (singular). Nāfiʿ, Ibn Kathīr, and al-Ḥasan read "al-riyāḥ" (plural). The majority read "fa-yaẓlalna" with a fatḥa on the lām, while Qatāda read "fa-yuẓlilna" with a kasra on the lām. The rest of the verse is clear: in it is admonition, and the honouring of the patient and grateful person by specifying them, and patience and gratitude together contain all good, and they cannot exist except in a world (of trial).

It is related that ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb, may Allah be pleased with him, was told: "The land has become barren and the people have despaired." He said: "Then they will be given rain," meaning that relief comes at the time of hardship.

The commentators differed concerning the words of the Exalted: ﴿and spreads His mercy﴾. One group said: by "mercy" He means rain, and He has enumerated one blessing with two expressions, the second of which emphasises the first. Another group said: the mercy in this place is the sun. This is then an enumeration of a different blessing from the first. The reason is that when rain falls after despair, it is well received, but when it continues it becomes wearisome, so the sun comes after it, which is of great benefit. The words of the Exalted: ﴿He is the Protector, the Praiseworthy﴾ mean that from these acts of His, He is the one who benefits when He is an ally, and His acts and blessings are praised, unlike those idols of yours that neither harm nor benefit.

Then the Exalted mentioned the greatest sign and the handiwork that points to the Maker, which is His creation of the heavens and the earth. As for the words of the Exalted: ﴿and of the living creatures He has dispersed in them﴾, this can be interpreted in several ways. One is that He means one of the two (heavens or earth) but mentions both, as the Exalted said: ﴿From both of them come forth pearls and coral﴾ (Qur'an 55:22), while in fact they come forth only from the salt water. Another is that Allah the Exalted created the heavens and dispersed creatures in them that we do not know. Another is that He means the animals found in the clouds, which sometimes occur, such as frogs and the like, since the cloud is included in the name "sky." Al-Ṭabarī related from Mujāhid that he said, in explaining the words ﴿and of the living creatures He has dispersed in them﴾, that they are humans and angels.

The Qāḍī Abū Muḥammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

It is far-fetched, and not in accordance with the usage of the language, for the word "dābba" (living creature) to apply to angels.

The words of the Exalted: ﴿And He is able to gather them﴾ mean: on the Day of Resurrection, at the gathering from the graves.

The words of the Exalted: ﴿Whatever affliction befalls you﴾: the majority of readers read "fa-bimā" with a fāʾ (so the reading is "fa-bimā kasabat"), and it is so in most of the codices. He said: "Because they know that Allah the Exalted is the One who tested them with their sins." Then the Exalted informed about the limitation and weakness of the son of Adam, and that he is within the grasp of power, that the pursuit of his Lord, mighty and majestic is He, cannot be frustrated, and that escape from Him is not possible for him.

"Al-Jawārī" is the plural of "jāriya," which means a ship. Nāfiʿ, ʿĀṣim, Abū Jaʿfar, and Shayba read "al-jawārī" with the yāʾ. Some retained it both in connection and at a pause on the rāʾ. ʿĀṣim also read it with the yāʾ omitted both in connection and at a pause. Abū Ḥātim said: "We retain it in every case." "Al-aʿlām" means mountains, and from it comes the saying of al-Khansāʾ:

*Indeed Ṣakhr, by him the rightly guided take their lead,*
*as if he were a beacon with fire at its top.*

And from it comes the proverb: "When they passed a mountain, another mountain appeared." So the sailing of ships on the water is a great sign, and the subjection of the wind for that is a blessing from Him, the Exalted. And if He willed to still the wind from them, they would remain motionless, that is, they would stand still and not move, and no purpose would be accomplished by them. Abū ʿAmr and ʿĀṣim read "al-rīḥ" (singular). Nāfiʿ, Ibn Kathīr, and al-Ḥasan read "al-riyāḥ" (plural). The majority read "fa-yaẓlalna" with a fatḥa on the lām, while Qatāda read "fa-yuẓlilna" with a kasra on the lām. The rest of the verse is clear: in it is admonition, and the honouring of the patient and grateful person by specifying them, and patience and gratitude together contain all good, and they cannot exist except in a world (of trial).

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 42, verses 34–38:

His, the Mighty and Majestic, saying:

﴿Or He may destroy them for what they have earned, and pardon much.﴾ ﴿And those who dispute concerning Our signs will know that they will have no place of escape.﴾ ﴿So whatever you have been given is but the enjoyment of worldly life; and what is with Allah is better and more lasting for those who believe and rely upon their Lord.﴾ ﴿And those who avoid the major sins (kaba'ir al-ithm) and immoralities, and when they are angry, they forgive.﴾ ﴿And those who have responded to their Lord, established prayer, and whose affair is [conducted by] consultation among themselves, and who spend from what We have provided them.﴾

Awbaqtu al-rajul (I destroyed the man): when I entangle him in a matter in which he perishes. Infiyaq in ships is their sinking. The pronoun in ﴿"kasabu"﴾ refers to the passengers of the ships from among mankind, meaning: for the sins of mankind. Then He, exalted is He, mentions again ﴿"and pardons much"﴾ for emphasis and clarification.

Nafi', Ibn 'Amir, al-A'raj, Abu Ja'far and Shayba read ﴿"wa-ya'lamu"﴾ with the nominative (raf'), as a resumption (qat' wa-istinaf, a new independent clause). This is good usage when it follows a conditional (jaza'). The rest of the readers and the majority read ﴿"wa-ya'lama"﴾ with the accusative (nasb), by the implicit presence of "an" (that). This wāw and similar ones are what the Kufans call "wāw al-sarf" (the wāw of diversion, lit. "wāw of transformation"), because the real function of wāw al-sarf is to coordinate a verb with a noun. "An" is then implied so that it forms, together with the verb, a verbal noun (masdar), and its conjunction with the noun becomes possible. An example is the poet's words:

﴿ ........................... ∗∗∗ تَقَضِّي لُباناتٍ ويَسْأمُ سائِمُ ﴾

It is as if he intended: "and weariness (sa'ama) of a weary one," so he implied "wa-an yasam" so that it would be in the sense of the verbal noun "sa'ama". Abu 'Ali said: the accusative is good when it is preceded by a condition and a consequence, and neither of them is obligatory.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿"ma lahum min mahis"﴾ (they have no place of escape) is their known fate, which He wished that those who dispute His signs, mighty and majestic is He, would know. Al-mahis (lit. "escape") is the refuge and the place of evasion. It is said: "haasa" when one evades. In the hadith of Heraclius: "فَحاصُوا حَيْصَةَ حُمْرِ الوَحْشِ إلى الأبْوابِ" ("so they fled in a rush like wild asses to the gates"). Then, exalted is He, admonished His servants, belittled in their sight the matter and affair of this world, and encouraged them towards what is with Him of blessings and the lofty station in His presence, and magnified the value of that in His saying: ﴿"So whatever you have been given of anything"﴾, the verse.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿"Those who avoid"﴾ is a coordination with His saying, exalted is He: "those who believe" (al-ladhina amanu). The majority of people read ﴿"kaba'ira"﴾ in the plural. Al-Hasan said: they are everything for which the Fire is threatened. Al-Dahhak said: or everything which carries a prescribed penalty (hadd) among the hudud. Ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with him, said: the kaba'ir are from the beginning of Surat al-Nisa' up to the end of about thirty verses. 'Ali ibn Abi Talib and Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, said: they are everything that Allah concludes with Fire, wrath, curse or punishment. Hamza, al-Kisa'i and 'Asim read ﴿"kabira"﴾ in the singular, as the noun of genus (ism al-jins). Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "kabir al-ithm" is shirk and immoralities. Al-Suddi said: it is adultery. Muqatil said: those things which necessitate the prescribed penalties. It is possible that "kabira" is a noun of genus with the meaning of "kaba'ir," so that the seven destructive sins (al-muwbiqat al-sab') enter into it, as their matter has been explained in other than this verse.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿"And when they are angry, they forgive"﴾ is an exhortation to suppress anger and to train oneself to extinguish it, for it is a flame (jamhara) from Hell and a gate of its gates. A man said to the Prophet ﷺ: "Advise me." He said: "Do not become angry." He said: "Increase [advice] for me." He said: "Do not become angry." He said: "Increase [advice] for me." He said: "Do not become angry." Whoever struggles against this disturbance within himself until he overcomes it, he has been spared a great concern in his worldly life and his Hereafter.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿"And those who have responded to their Lord"﴾ is a praise of everyone who believes in Allah, exalted is He, and accepts His law. He, exalted is He, praised the people whose affair is [conducted by] consultation among themselves, because in that is the unity of word, mutual love, the joining of hands and mutual support in goodness. In a hadith: "No people consult together except that they are guided to the best of what is before them." His saying, exalted is He: ﴿"and from what We have provided them, they spend"﴾ means: in the way of Allah, in accordance with the form of the law and within its limits, in the moderation which Allah, exalted is He, praised in other than this verse.

Ibn Zayd said: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿"And those who have responded to their Lord"﴾, the verse, was revealed concerning the Ansar. The apparent meaning is that Allah, exalted is He, praised everyone who is characterized by this attribute, whoever he may be. Did the Ansar attain this attribute except after the Muhajirun had preceded them to it? May Allah, exalted is He, be pleased with all of them by His grace.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 42, verses 39–41:

The Exalted said:

﴿And those who, when wrongful oppression afflicts them, defend themselves.﴾ ﴿And the recompense of an evil is an evil like it; but whoever pardons and makes reconciliation, his reward is upon Allah. Indeed, He does not love the wrongdoers.﴾ ﴿And whoever defends himself after being wronged, those—there is no blame upon them.﴾

In this verse, Allah the Exalted praises a people for retaliating against oppression. Some of the scholars preferred this view and said: "Retaliating against wrongdoing with what is obligatory is changing an evil; and whoever does not retaliate, while retaliation is possible, has abandoned changing the evil."

People differed about the intended meaning of the verse, although they agreed that whoever is oppressed and wronged is permitted to defend himself by means of the hand of truth and the ruler of the Muslims. Muqatil said: the verse concerns the wounded person who takes equal retribution from the one who wounded him, by way of qisas (retaliation in kind).

Another group said: it was revealed concerning the aggression of a polytheist against a believer. Allah the Exalted permitted him to defend himself against them without transgression, and pardon and reconciliation were linked to a reward. Then that was abrogated (naskh) by the verse of the sword. This group, which is the majority (al-jumhur), said: if a believer transgresses against another believer and wrongs him, the other is not permitted to take redress from him himself and repay him for his wrongdoing. An example of this is: a person betrays another, then the first person becomes able to betray the one who betrayed him. The position of Malik, may Allah have mercy on him, is that he should not do so, and this is the position of a great community alongside him. They did not take this verse in this sense, and they argued with the saying of the Prophet ﷺ: "Return the trust to the one who entrusted you, and do not betray the one who betrayed you." This statement is more pure and closer to Allah, blessed and exalted.

A group of the people of knowledge said: this verse is general concerning polytheists and believers, and whoever is oppressed and wronged is permitted to take redress for himself, and to betray whoever betrayed him in wealth until he gets his right from him. They said that the hadith "and do not betray the one who betrayed you" is only concerning "a man who asked the Messenger of Allah ﷺ: May he commit adultery with the wife of the one who committed adultery with his wife? The Prophet ﷺ said to him: That is what he intends by adultery."

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

Likewise the hadith has come in the sense of adultery, as the narrators have mentioned; but as for its generality, it extends to everything.

As for His saying: ﴿And the recompense of an evil is an evil like it﴾, al-Zajjaj said: He named the punishment by the name of the sin.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This is when we take "evil" in the right of Allah the Exalted to mean disobedience, since recompense from Allah the Exalted is not an evil unless it is named by the name of what causes it. But if we take "evil" in the sense of calamity in the right of human beings, that is, this harms this one and the other harms him, then we do not need to say "he named the punishment by the name of the sin"; rather the first act and the last act are both an evil. Ibn Abi Najih and al-Suddi said: the meaning of the verse is that if a man is insulted with an insult, he may return it in the same manner without exceeding it. al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan said: so long as it is not a slander (hadd) or a grave disgrace.

The lam in His saying: ﴿And whoever defends himself﴾ is the lam of the oath-introduction (lam al-iltiqa' al-qasam). His saying: ﴿there is no way against them﴾ means: no way of blame, and no way of judgment. This is a clear statement of the permissibility of retaliation, and there is disagreement about it: is it between a believer and a polytheist, or between believers, as has preceded?

"ʿAzm al-umur" (the matters requiring determination) means its firm and perfected matters, and the praiseworthy outcome of them.

The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "When it is the Day of Resurrection, a caller will call out: Whoever has a reward with Allah, let him stand. A multitude of people will stand, and it will be said to them: What is your reward? They will say: We are those who pardoned when we were wronged in the world."

Then Allah, Exalted, described to His Prophet Muhammad ﷺ their condition on the Day of Resurrection when they see the punishment. He singled out from their description and the description of their state that they say: ﴿Is there any way to return?﴾ This statement indicates the evil of what they have come to know. "Al-maradd" (the return): the subject of returning to the world. The meaning they intended is that there be a return, so that they could make up for their deeds and faith. The seeing in this verse is seeing with the eye (ruʾyat ʿayn).

Ṭalḥa ibn Muṣarrif read "mina l-dhull" with a kasra on the dhāl. "Al-khushūʿ" (humility) is submissiveness, and it may be praiseworthy; what brings it to the state of blame is His saying ﴿"mina l-dhull"﴾. Accordingly, the connection of "min" to "khāshiʿīn" is strengthened.

Some people said, as al-Ṭabarī related: Since they will be gathered blind, and their gaze is with the eyes of their hearts, He made it a hidden glance, meaning their gaze does not appear.

In this interpretation there is strain.

Qatada and al-Suddi said: The meaning is that they steal glances, since they are in such grief and bad condition that they cannot look with the whole eye, but look only with part of it. Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 42, verses 46–48:

His, the Exalted and Majestic, saying:

﴿And they will have no allies to help them against God. And whomever God leaves astray, for him there is no way.﴾ ﴿Respond to your Lord before there comes a Day from God which cannot be turned back. For you there will be no refuge that day, nor will you have any denial.﴾ ﴿But if they turn away, We have not sent you as a guardian over them. Your duty is only to deliver the message. And when We let man taste mercy from Us, he rejoices in it; but if an evil befalls them for what their hands have sent forward, then indeed man is ungrateful.﴾

His saying, "And they will have no allies": this is a rebuke against the idols and images whose allegiance the disbelievers displayed and whose devotion they held as a religion. The meaning: why do they take as allies these things that neither harm nor benefit? But whomever God leaves astray, for him there is no way of guidance and salvation.

Then God, the Exalted, commanded His Prophet ﷺ to order them to respond to the call of God and His law, and warned them of the coming of the Day of Resurrection, after which no one will be returned to works, and in which there is no refuge or escape for anyone, except through knowledge of God, the Exalted, and righteous deeds in this world. So He informed them that for them there is no refuge and no "nakir" (denial). (p-528) "Nakir" is a verbal noun meaning denial, and it is like "adhir al-hayy" and similar verbal nouns. It is also possible that it is a form of the active participle from "nakira," though the meaning is far from that, because "nakira" essentially means he did not discern and thought the matter was other than what he had known.

His saying, "But if they turn away, We have not sent you as a guardian over them": this is a comfort to Muhammad ﷺ and a removal of his concern for them, and He informed him that his duty is only to deliver the message to them and convey the proof. Then the phrase in the rest of the verse comes in the manner of saying: "and the people are a people of insolence, inconsistency of character, and instability; when they are given mercy they rejoice in it and become insolent, and if an evil afflicts them, that is, a calamity that distresses them in their bodies or souls, because of their sins and ugly deeds, then they become disbelievers at that time, impatient." He expressed it with "man" (al-insan), which is a general term, so that all disbelievers among the neighbors of that time and others are included in the preceding verse. The plural pronoun in His saying, "tusibhum" (afflicts them), refers back to the word "al-insan" insofar as it is a collective noun encompassing many.

(p-529) ﴿To God belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth. He creates what He wills. He bestows females on whom He wills, and He bestows males on whom He wills﴾ ﴿Or He pairs them, males and females, and He makes whom He wills barren. Indeed He is All-Knowing, All-Powerful﴾ ﴿It is not for a human that God should speak to him except by revelation (wahy), or from behind a veil, or by sending a messenger who reveals, by His permission, what He wills. Indeed He is Most High, All-Wise﴾ ﴿And thus We have revealed to you a spirit (rooh) from Our command. You did not know what the Book was, nor what faith was, but We made it a light by which We guide whom We will of Our servants. And indeed you guide to a straight path﴾ ﴿The path of God, to whom belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth. Unquestionably, to God all affairs are returned﴾

The first verse is a verse of reflection (i'tibar), indicating the power and the all-encompassing dominion over creation, and that His will, glorified and exalted is He, is effective over all His creation and in all their affairs. There is no place for an idol in this, for the One who creates what He wills and originates is none other than God, glorified is He. He is the One who apportions creation, so He bestows females upon whomever He wills to make his offspring women, and bestows males upon whomever He wills in this manner. Or He varies them: at one time He bestows a male, and at another time a female. This is the meaning of His words, exalted is He: ﴿Or He pairs them﴾. Muhammad ibn al-Hanafiyya said: by His words ﴿Or He pairs them﴾ He means twins, that is, He places in one womb a pair of offspring, a male and a female. "Al-'aqim" (the barren) is the one to whom no child is born. All of this is governed by knowledge and power. And this verse necessitates the impossibility of the existence of the ambiguous hermaphrodite (al-khunthā al-mushkil).

In this verse, exalted is He, began with mentioning females, to show them affection and honour, so that they would be cared for, protected and treated kindly. This was related from him by al-Tha'labi. Ishaq ibn Bishr said: this verse was revealed concerning the prophets, peace be upon them, and then it was generalised. Lot, peace be upon him, was the father of daughters, to whom no son was born; Abraham, peace be upon him, was the opposite of him; Muhammad ﷺ was given both kinds; and Yahya ibn Zakariyya, peace be upon both of them, was barren.
